input_signals.name: Dilutive issuance into accumulated deficit
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, at), 1), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Equity issuance is far worse news when retained earnings are deeply negative, because the proceeds fund past losses rather than new projects; investors underreact to the dilution-plus-deficit combination.
input_signals.reasoning: Retained earnings scaled by assets is a classic accumulated-distress state variable (Z-score component), and issuance by such firms is closer to a survival financing event than to opportunistic growth capital. Weighting the issuance intensity by the cross-sectional rank of accumulated deficit lets the same dollar of issuance carry a stronger negative loading for distressed issuers while remaining continuous and fully covered.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sstk, at ), 1 ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Distressed deleveraging recovery
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 1), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(ib, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement by highly levered, low-profit firms signals successful balance-sheet repair and falling default probability, and the resolution of distress risk is rewarded with high subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: For healthy firms debt repayment is a mundane capital-structure choice, but for distressed firms it is a credible, cash-verified reduction in bankruptcy likelihood that equity holders capture with high leverage. The SUMRANK distress score combines solvency (lt/at) and profitability (ib/at) so the financing flow is amplified only where default risk is genuinely priced.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( dltr, dltis ), at ), 1 ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( ib, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Share dilution into accumulated deficit
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(GROWTH(csho, 1), 1), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Dilution measured by shares outstanding, rather than by reported issuance proceeds, is the economically complete measure of claim transfer, and it is most damaging for firms whose retained earnings are deeply negative because equity is being sold to fund accumulated losses.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-0 dilution-into-deficit signal delivered both a negative slope and a reliable FF5 alpha but covered only 13% of firm-months because sstk is sparsely reported; csho growth captures the same economic dilution with near-universal balance-sheet coverage. Comparing the two isolates whether the earlier result was a measurement artifact of issuance reporting or a genuine dilution-under-distress effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Buybacks against a liquidity constraint
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(prstkc, at), 1), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dltt, at), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Repurchasing stock while carrying heavy long-term debt and negative working capital is the most expensive possible undervaluation signal, because it consumes the very liquidity buffer that protects the firm from default, so only managers with strong private information do it.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen-0 pooled repurchases with dividends and found nothing, but the two payouts differ sharply in signaling content: dividends are sticky and habitual while buybacks are discretionary and timing-driven. Isolating prstkc and conditioning on a debt-plus-working-capital constraint tests a signaling channel that the pooled payout measure could not detect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( prstkc, at ), 1 ), rank( sumrank( ratio( dltt, at ), neg( ratio( wcap, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt versus internal funding tilt
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is the source mix of funds: levered firms covering their needs with new debt rather than with internally generated cash are the ones whose equity is most exposed to future credit tightening, and they underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: The tilt construction (difference of two ranks scaled by a distress rank) produced the cleanest, most statistically reliable portfolio spread in the archive, but it was applied to the equity-versus-debt margin, which turned out to be factor-explained. Applying the same well-behaved structure to the economically distinct debt-versus-internal-funds margin keeps the portfolio properties while switching to the channel where genuine FF5 alpha appeared.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Net borrowing into deteriorating earnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 1), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(ib, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Levering up while profitability is actively deteriorating is a pro-cyclical financing mistake: the new debt is contracted against earnings that are already falling, so equity value is subsequently written down.
input_signals.reasoning: All prior conditioning used the *level* of distress, which is highly persistent and largely priced; the change in profitability identifies firms transitioning into distress, where financing decisions are least likely to be already reflected in prices. This isolates the conditioning dimension — state versus transition — while holding the net-borrowing financing measure fixed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ), 1 ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( ib, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Unfunded borrowing with accumulated deficit
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Borrowing that exceeds a firm's own cash generation is most damaging when the balance sheet already carries high liabilities and a history of accumulated losses, because the new debt services the past rather than funding the future.
input_signals.reasoning: The debt-versus-internal-funding tilt scaled by a single leverage rank is the archive's only design with a significant slope and a significant negative alpha, so the productive refinement is to strengthen the conditioning variable rather than the financing leg. Adding accumulated deficit to leverage builds a two-component distress state (stock solvency plus loss history) that avoids reusing oancf, which already appears in the financing tilt.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Borrowing beyond earnings capacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(ib, at))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Earnings, not cash flow, is the benchmark lenders and equity holders capitalize; levered firms whose new borrowing ranks far above their profitability rank are contracting fixed claims their income cannot support and underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing oancf with ib holds the tilt structure and distress leg fixed while isolating two design choices at once: the measurement of internal funds, and coverage, since cash-flow-statement items cut usable observations from 0.126 to 0.088. If the slope and alpha survive with materially higher coverage, the mechanism is about income capacity rather than about the cash-flow reporting subsample.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( ib, at ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Borrowing without tax-shield capacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(txt, at), RATIO(pi, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms with no pretax income and no tax payments obtain no tax-shield benefit from debt, so their borrowing must be need-driven rather than optimizing, and that necessity is the component of debt issuance the market misprices.
input_signals.reasoning: This reframes the conditioning variable from "how distressed" to "why would this firm rationally borrow", using the tax variables that no prior proposal touched; a zero-tax, zero-pretax-income borrower is almost definitionally financing a shortfall. If it outperforms the leverage-based conditioning, it identifies the motive rather than the state as the source of the alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( ratio( txt, at ), ratio( pi, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding gap with no liquidity buffer
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(act, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Borrowing in excess of internally generated cash is most informative when the firm has no near-term liquidity cushion, because only then is the debt draw unambiguously a response to an imminent funding shortfall rather than a financing choice.
input_signals.reasoning: The liquidity-buffer conditioning produced the strongest and most reliable alpha in the archive (−0.056, t −4.08) but a flat slope because its financing leg counted all borrowing as bad; the funding-gap tilt fixes precisely that by subtracting the benign, cash-generating borrower. Crossing the best-performing conditioning variable with the best-performing financing leg is the highest-value consolidation available.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( ratio( che, lct ), ratio( act, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding gap against a three-part distress score
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at)), NEG(RATIO(che, lct))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency, loss history, and liquidity are distinct components of financial fragility, and an unfunded debt draw is worst for firms scoring badly on all three simultaneously.
input_signals.reasoning: The two-component score (leverage plus accumulated deficit) gave the best joint result so far, and the single-component liquidity score gave the best alpha, suggesting the components carry complementary information rather than overlapping information. Aggregating three ranked channels should place the short leg on firms that are unambiguously fragile, which is where a funding gap should be most severely penalized.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), sumrank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ), neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Coverage-repaired unfunded borrowing
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ib, at)))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The unfunded-borrowing mechanism is about internal funds generally, so firms without a reported cash-flow statement can be measured with earnings, extending the same economic signal to a much larger sample.
input_signals.reasoning: The best signal in the archive is confined to 8.8% of firm-months because oancf is sparsely populated, while the earnings-benchmarked variant reached 12.6% coverage but with roughly half the alpha; using cash flow where available and earnings only as a fallback should preserve the stronger measure while restoring coverage. This isolates whether the alpha differential between the two variants was a measurement effect or a sample-composition effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( coalesce( ratio( oancf, at ), ratio( ib, at ) ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry-neutral funding gap in distress
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at)))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Normal reliance on external debt differs enormously across industries, so a funding gap is only evidence of distress-driven borrowing when it is large relative to industry peers.
input_signals.reasoning: Capital-intensive and regulated industries borrow continuously against stable cash flows, so an unadjusted funding-gap rank loads mechanically on industry membership, diluting the distress interpretation and adding sector risk to the long-short spread. Industry-demeaning the financing leg should raise the slope and improve the Sharpe by removing a sector bet while keeping the same economic mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Net debt intake beyond internal funds
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(act, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What burdens an illiquid firm is the net increase in debt claims beyond what operations can fund; gross issuance overstates the burden for firms that are simultaneously retiring maturing debt.
input_signals.reasoning: Every funding-gap winner used gross issuance, so the net-versus-gross choice has never been tested with the liquidity conditioning that produces the best alpha and Sharpe. If the net measure improves both statistics, the mechanism is genuine leverage escalation; if it degrades them, the mechanism is rollover activity, which sharpens interpretation for the final generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( ratio( che, lct ), ratio( act, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt-burden-scaled funding gap
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, lt)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Refinancing pressure is determined by new borrowing and cash generation measured against the existing liability stack, not against total assets, because it is liabilities that impose the fixed claims.
input_signals.reasoning: All prior gap constructions scaled both legs by assets, which mixes asset-heavy low-leverage firms into the extreme buckets; deflating by total liabilities makes the gap a coverage-shortfall measure directly comparable across capital structures. This isolates the scaling choice while holding the mechanism and the liquidity conditioning fixed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, lt ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, lt ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding gap versus persistent cash generation
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(act, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The right benchmark for new borrowing is the firm's sustainable cash-generating capacity rather than a single year's cash flow, which can be temporarily depressed by working-capital swings.
input_signals.reasoning: Single-year oancf noise is the most likely reason the gap's slope and alpha have never peaked in the same specification: transitory cash-flow dips misclassify healthy borrowers as distressed ones. A three-year average defines the internal-funds state more reliably, which should raise the cross-sectional slope without sacrificing the tail alpha the liquidity conditioning delivers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( ratio( che, lct ), ratio( act, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Borrowing into the cash account amid burn
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), NEG(RATIO(oancf, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a cash-burning firm borrows and the proceeds land in the cash account rather than in operations or investment, the draw is precautionary or lender-mandated liquidity insurance, which reveals that management fears losing access to funding.
input_signals.reasoning: Every prior design asked whether borrowing was justified; none asked where the money went, yet the use of proceeds is what distinguishes investment borrowing from defensive hoarding. Pairing a rise in cash with negative operating cash flow identifies drawn revolvers and precautionary raises, a distinct and previously untested economic channel.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( sumrank( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ), neg( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Distributions financed externally under strain
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Paying dividends and buying back stock in excess of internally generated cash, while leverage is high and cash thin, transfers value from creditors to shareholders in a way that is unsustainable and is followed by low equity returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Earlier payout tests treated distributions as an unconditional strength signal and failed, but the funding-gap logic implies that distributions matter only relative to the cash available to fund them. This applies the archive's proven gap-versus-internal-funds structure to the payout channel, reversing the sign expectation and testing whether the earlier payout failures came from ignoring how the payout was financed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( add( dvt, prstkc ), at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry-neutral gap with liquidity conditioning
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at)))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(act, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress-driven borrowing is identified by a funding gap that is abnormal relative to the firm's industry, combined with the absence of a liquidity cushion.
input_signals.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the gap preserved slope and alpha while removing a sector bet (gen-4 S6), and liquidity conditioning independently produced the best alpha and Sharpe (gen-4 S1); the two refinements address different sources of noise and have not been combined. If both effects are additive this should dominate the current frontier on slope, alpha reliability, and Sharpe simultaneously.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( ratio( che, lct ), ratio( act, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding gap against a maturity wall
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, at), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Unfunded borrowing is most dangerous for firms with a large stock of debt maturing within the year and no cash to meet it, because refusal by a single lender then forces default.
input_signals.reasoning: All prior conditioning used solvency, profitability, or liquidity levels; none used the near-term maturity structure, yet the timing of claims is what converts illiquidity into default. Pairing short-term debt intensity with cash scarcity targets exactly the population for which new borrowing is a rollover necessity rather than a choice.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( dlc, at ), neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding gap inside the illiquid subsample
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), INDICATOR(RATIO(lct, act), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The funding-gap effect exists only among firms whose current liabilities exceed current assets; within that group the gap should separate rescue borrowers from self-funding firms, while outside it financing choices are uninformative.
input_signals.reasoning: Continuous rank weighting still lets healthy firms populate the extreme portfolios and dilutes both legs, whereas the hard indicator forces the long and short baskets to be drawn from the same distressed population, isolating the interaction rather than mixing it with a distress main effect. This is the cleanest available test of whether the mechanism is truly conditional and it should improve the alpha per unit of turnover if it is.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), indicator( ratio( lct, act ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Gap scaled by worst fragility dimension
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(MIN(RATIO(ib, lt), RATIO(che, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial fragility is determined by a firm's weakest dimension, not by an average of dimensions: a firm fails if either its earnings cannot service debt or its cash cannot meet current obligations.
input_signals.reasoning: Every multi-component distress score so far used SUMRANK, which averages and therefore lets strength on one dimension offset fatal weakness on another — plausibly why the three-part score underperformed the single liquidity measure on alpha. Using MIN implements the economically correct weakest-link logic with a distinct operator, and it separates earnings-based and liquidity-based fragility rather than blending them.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( min( ratio( ib, lt ), ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Borrowing as working capital erodes
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: It is the deterioration of liquidity, not its level, that makes an unfunded debt draw informative: firms whose working capital is shrinking while they borrow are financing a live, worsening shortfall.
input_signals.reasoning: Level-based liquidity conditioning delivers reliable alpha but is highly persistent and largely known to the market, whereas the change in working capital is new information arriving with the same filing as the borrowing. This tests the state-versus-transition conditioning choice within the best-performing financing leg, an axis where earlier transition tests used earnings and sales rather than liquidity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap with current-ratio erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The mechanism is deterioration in the net current position while the firm draws new debt; measuring that position directly from current assets and current liabilities captures the same economics as reported working capital for a wider set of firms.
input_signals.reasoning: The best signal in the archive is limited to 7.1% of firm-months, partly because wcap is a less consistently populated field than its two components. Reconstructing the change in net current assets from act and lct is an exact economic substitute and tests whether the effect survives, or strengthens, on a broader sample — the single most useful robustness check available for the new leader.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( sub( act, lct ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap with eroding and thin liquidity
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1), RATIO(che, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: An unfunded debt draw is most alarming for a firm whose liquidity is both low in level and falling, since neither the buffer nor the trend can absorb the next shortfall.
input_signals.reasoning: Liquidity level conditioning and liquidity change conditioning each independently produced alphas near −0.04 to −0.05 with correct-signed slopes, and they describe logically distinct states, so their combination may identify a strictly more fragile population than either alone. This directly tests whether the two liquidity dimensions are complements or substitutes, which determines the final specification.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ), ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap with twin deterioration
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(ib, at), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Borrowing is most damaging when both the liquidity position and profitability are deteriorating in the same year, because the firm is losing the two resources — cushion and earnings — that service the new claims.
input_signals.reasoning: The two transition variables tested separately gave the archive's strongest slope (earnings change, t −3.34) and its strongest portfolio evidence (working-capital change, alpha −0.053), suggesting each captures a different facet of an ongoing deterioration. Building a purely transition-based distress score should retain the slope from earnings and the portfolio power from liquidity, addressing the persistent slope-versus-alpha trade-off with economics rather than with rescaling.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ), delta( ratio( ib, at ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry-neutral gap with erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A funding gap is evidence of distress-driven borrowing only relative to industry financing norms, and combining that adjustment with liquidity erosion should isolate firm-specific funding stress.
input_signals.reasoning: Industry demeaning of the financing leg previously preserved alpha while improving the slope and removing a sector bet, and it has never been paired with the erosion conditioning that now defines the frontier. If the Sharpe rises above −0.553 the improvement is attributable to sector-risk removal rather than to a different economic population.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap with cash drawdown
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If liquidity erosion is what matters, then a falling cash balance despite new borrowing is the most severe case, because the firm is losing cash faster than the credit market is supplying it.
input_signals.reasoning: An earlier test found that borrowing *into* a rising cash balance amid operating losses also predicted low returns (alpha −0.034), which is the opposite balance-sheet movement, so the two designs together determine whether the signal is about hoarding or about depletion. Resolving that ambiguity is essential before committing the final generations to a use-of-proceeds interpretation of the mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Coverage-repaired gap with erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ib, at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The mechanism is borrowing in excess of internal funds while liquidity erodes, and internal funds can be proxied by earnings where a cash-flow statement is unavailable, extending the same signal to a substantially larger sample.
input_signals.reasoning: The leader covers only 7.1% of firm-months, and when this same fallback was applied under static solvency conditioning the alpha halved, but that test cannot distinguish a measurement effect from the weakness of the static conditioner. Rerunning it against the erosion conditioner is the decisive coverage test: if alpha and slope both hold near the leader's level, the final signal can be specified on nearly twice the sample.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( coalesce( ratio( oancf, at ), ratio( ib, at ) ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Total debt intake with erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltis, DELTA(dlc, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Liquidity-stressed firms fund shortfalls through revolvers and other short-term facilities as much as through term debt, so the complete measure of new borrowing is long-term issuance plus the increase in debt in current liabilities.
input_signals.reasoning: Every version of the financing leg so far counted only dltis, which mechanically omits precisely the borrowing channel most used under working-capital stress — exactly the population the erosion conditioner selects. Adding the change in current debt should strengthen both the slope and the alpha if the mechanism is genuine funding pressure rather than a term-debt-market phenomenon.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( add( dltis, delta( dlc, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Erosion and scarcity double conditioning
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Unfunded borrowing is most severely mispriced for firms that are simultaneously low on cash and losing working capital, since only they face an unavoidable near-term funding decision.
input_signals.reasoning: Averaging the level and change of liquidity through SUMRANK gave a slightly weaker alpha than the change alone (−0.049 versus −0.053), which suggests averaging dilutes rather than that the level is uninformative; a multiplicative stack instead requires both conditions to hold and so concentrates the short leg. This isolates the aggregation operator — averaged versus multiplicative conditioning — as the design choice under test.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap with obligation-scaled erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically relevant deterioration is in working capital measured against near-term obligations, because a given dollar decline matters far more for a firm with large current liabilities.
input_signals.reasoning: Scaling the erosion by total assets treats a dollar of lost working capital identically for firms with very different current-liability loads, blurring the severity dimension that should determine the size of the mispricing. Deflating by lct makes the conditioner a change in current-ratio-like coverage, a small but economically motivated sharpening of the archive's strongest conditioning variable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Total intake with obligation-scaled erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltis, DELTA(dlc, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Complete new borrowing — term issuance plus the increase in current debt — measured against internal cash generation, is most informative when net current assets are shrinking relative to the near-term obligations they must cover.
input_signals.reasoning: These are the two individually best-performing components of the mechanism: obligation-scaled erosion gave the archive's most reliable alpha (t −3.77) and total debt intake gave the best Sharpe among financing-leg variants (−0.529), and they modify different parts of the expression so their effects should compound. This is the leading candidate for the final specification.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( add( dltis, delta( dlc, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap with dual liquidity erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1), DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Liquidity erosion is better identified by two independent balance-sheet channels — the net current position relative to obligations and the cash balance — because each contains reporting noise the other does not.
input_signals.reasoning: The working-capital and cash-drawdown conditioners performed almost identically on their own (alpha −0.051 and −0.045, t −3.77 and −3.62) yet are measured from different accounts, so averaging their ranks should cancel idiosyncratic accrual noise while reinforcing the common deterioration signal. Cash also has better data availability, which should lift coverage above 0.071.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ) ), rank( neg( sumrank( delta( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ), delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gap against scarcest internal resource
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(MIN(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(che, at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm can avoid distress borrowing only if it has both cash flow and cash reserves, so its internal funding capacity is set by whichever of the two is scarcer.
input_signals.reasoning: Adding the cash stock to the benchmark produced the largest alpha in the entire archive (−0.059) but a slope of only −1.45, because the persistent, widely dispersed cash rank overwhelmed the flow in the rank blend; taking the minimum of the two levels keeps the binding-constraint economics while letting cash matter only when it is genuinely the scarcer resource. This is the last untried fix for the archive's one remaining slope-versus-alpha trade-off.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( min( ratio( oancf, at ), ratio( che, at ) ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Broad-sample gap with obligation erosion
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ib, at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The unfunded-borrowing-under-erosion effect should exist wherever internal funds can be measured, with earnings serving as the benchmark when no cash-flow statement is reported.
input_signals.reasoning: The earnings fallback lifted coverage from 0.071 to 0.103 and produced the strongest slope among erosion designs (−3.11) but a diluted alpha (−0.032) when paired with asset-scaled erosion; pairing it instead with the more reliable obligation-scaled conditioner tests whether a materially broader, more investable version of the signal can retain economically meaningful abnormal returns. A usable compromise between coverage and alpha is worth documenting in the final round.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sub( rank( ratio( dltis, at ) ), rank( coalesce( ratio( oancf, at ), ratio( ib, at ) ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( wcap, lct ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Sector-neutral erosion gap
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RANK(RATIO(dltis, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, at)))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(wcap, lct), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress-driven borrowing is defined relative to industry financing norms, and removing the industry component of the funding gap should leave a cleaner, less sector-exposed spread.
input_signals.reasoning: Industry demeaning previously preserved alpha reliability (t −3.55) while removing a sector bet, and it has not been paired with the obligation-scaled erosion conditioner that now carries the strongest portfolio evidence. As the final robustness check, it establishes whether the mechanism is a firm-level funding phenomenon rather than a disguised industry tilt.
